items.title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini Decisions API for fast, calibrated multimodal decision-making across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Google DeepMind has introduced the Gemini Decisions API, powered by the Gemini Decision 1 model, enabling rapid evaluation of up to 1,000 yes/no, multiple choice, and rubric-scoring questions in a single pass across various data types including text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. The API provides confidence scores for each decision, supporting applications like content grading, policy checks, and query routing with low latency and cost efficiency. The Gemini Decision 1 model processes multimodal inputs natively and returns probabilistic scores without token-by-token decoding, achieving 150-250 ms end-to-end latency and costing $0.10 per million input tokens with no output token charges. It supports combined modalities in one request and offers three decision types-yes/no, multiple choice, and ordered rubric scoring-each with confidence metrics to facilitate fallback or human review. The API is accessible via Google AI Studio with documentation for Python, JavaScript, and REST.

items.title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights citing security and regulatory concerns [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: United Airlines announced it is prohibiting artificial intelligence agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers due to security risks and potential violations of federal regulations. The airline highlighted concerns about sharing personal account credentials with third-party AI assistants, which could lead to unintended purchases or account changes. United is updating its booking and ticketing policies to restrict AI agent access both directly and through travel agencies and aggregators. The airline aims to maintain control over the booking process and avoid additional costs associated with AI-driven flight searches. Other airlines, like Southwest, have taken different approaches by integrating AI access to flight inventories, but United will continue to allow bookings through traditional aggregators such as Kayak and Google Flights.

items.title: Researcher uses AI agents to analyze NASA lidar data and identifies a Maya archaeological site in Mexico not listed in the official INAH register
items.content_text: A researcher employed multiple AI agents to analyze NASA lidar data covering 1,200 square kilometers of jungle in Mexico, identifying a Maya site with distinct architectural features that was not registered by Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH). The process took less than 72 hours from initial idea to official communication with INAH. The AI agents converted lidar data into images and systematically examined them for man-made structures, filtering out natural formations. After confirming the site's features and preparing a detailed report, the researcher contacted INAH, which initially confirmed no registered site at that location. However, it was later revealed that the site had been previously mapped in academic literature but was not included in INAH's public register, indicating the agents rediscovered rather than discovered the site.

items.title: Atuin launches Threads to sync and search AI agent sessions across machines with end-to-end encryption [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Atuin has introduced Threads, a feature that allows users to search, sync, and resume AI agent sessions across multiple devices while preserving full context and history. This extension of Atuin's encrypted sync engine supports various agents like Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Omp, and OpenCode, enabling seamless continuation of tasks on different machines. Threads captures complete agent session data, including commands, outputs, and user intent, stored locally and optionally synced via Atuin's hosted or self-hosted servers with end-to-end encryption. The feature also includes an MCP tool that lets agents reference past sessions to build on previous work, improving efficiency and collaboration across environments.

items.title: Apple researchers present neural network method to speed up maximum inner product search for retrieval-augmented generation, improving efficiency and accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Apple researchers introduced a new approach using small neural networks trained offline to accelerate maximum inner product search (MIPS), a key operation in recommendation systems, search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Their method learns to route queries more efficiently to their best matches, trading upfront training cost for faster and more accurate retrieval during inference. Traditional MIPS methods rely on clustering keys and routing queries based on centroids, which can cause errors and inefficiencies, especially since queries and keys differ significantly in nature. The researchers leverage the mathematical concept of the support function and input convex neural networks to approximate MIPS more effectively by learning from typical query distributions rather than generic assumptions. This approach promises to reduce computational costs in large-scale systems with millions of keys and high-dimensional vectors, potentially enhancing the performance of AI applications that depend on fast and precise retrieval of relevant information.

items.title: Pomerado launches platform to create APIs for any website in minutes, enabling AI agents to interact with legacy sites without direct access [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Pomerado, a startup founded by ex-McKinsey and Scale AI employees, has developed a self-serve platform that allows developers to generate APIs for any website, even those they do not own, within minutes. This enables AI agents to perform tasks on legacy websites and apps that lack APIs or modern interfaces, improving automation workflows in sectors like airlines, banking, and e-commerce. The platform creates deterministic machine-comprehensible protocols (MCPs) that speed up repeated tasks and handle authentication and two-factor authentication securely. The system works by having an AI agent explore a website and perform a task once, recording the interactions to build a generalizable API. A Guardian model reviews the process to ensure compliance with guardrails, and maintenance jobs automatically fix or improve the API if future runs fail. Pomerado offers both an open-source version and a free hosted service, with users including personal trainers, car dealerships, and personal assistants who benefit from more reliable and faster automation compared to traditional browser automation or computer use.

items.title: Researchers find reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons in large language models can backdoor AI agents without training, enabling hidden triggers to execute attacker code [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have discovered that altering fewer than 10 dormant neurons in a large language model (LLM) can implant a backdoor that remains inactive until triggered, allowing the model to execute malicious code without affecting normal behavior. This attack, named Lazarus, requires no additional training and can be triggered by simple signals such as a date change, posing a significant security risk for AI agents built on these models. The attack exploits rarely firing neurons that can be reprogrammed to detect specific triggers and inject malicious commands during inference. Detection is challenging without comparing model weights to original versions, highlighting the importance of model provenance and integrity. Microsoft's Foundry system currently provides protections by verifying model sources and scanning containers, but the risk remains if trusted providers are compromised. The researchers emphasize that model weights require scrutiny similar to software code and advocate for layered defenses including provenance verification, weight auditing, and monitoring of AI agent behavior.

items.title: Pundit Claims launches open-source AI claims register evaluating Gary Marcus and Ed Zitron's statements with AI consensus and evidence levels [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Pundit Claims has introduced an open-source register that assesses AI-related claims made by Gary Marcus and Ed Zitron, categorizing them based on evidence strength and agreement between two independent AI systems. The register classifies claims as supported, mixed, contradicted, unresolved, or uncheckable, and distinguishes between claims and predictions, providing detailed statistics on accuracy and consensus levels. The evaluation includes thousands of claims and predictions, with a majority of Gary Marcus's claims rated as mostly right, supported by 88% to 90% consensus, while Ed Zitron's claims show a more balanced accuracy. The register highlights areas such as reliability, capabilities, and regulation policy, noting which claims are supported or contradicted, and tracks unresolved and uncheckable statements. This tool aims to provide a transparent, AI-driven fact-checking resource for AI discourse.

items.title: DeepMind launches AlphaGenome 2 to predict DNA variant effects on gene expression across hundreds of human cell types using over 100 million single-cell profiles [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: DeepMind announced AlphaGenome 2, a next-generation model that predicts how DNA sequences and their variations impact specific human cell types, enhancing understanding of disease mechanisms. The model uses a conditional architecture to analyze DNA effects in individual cell types and states, improving variant effect predictions compared to previous models. Trained on more than 107 million single-cell profiles from 68 tissues, AlphaGenome 2 can predict gene expression, chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, and DNA methylation at the cell-type level. It adapts to new single-cell data without retraining and is available for non-commercial research via an API, with commercial access in private preview. By resolving activity in specialized cells rather than broad tissue averages, AlphaGenome 2 helps researchers identify disease-relevant genetic variants that may be missed by earlier models, potentially advancing studies in rare diseases, complex traits, and fundamental biology.

items.title: Beaker autonomously edits language model weights to improve math problem accuracy by up to 30 points without running the model [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers demonstrated that Beaker, an autonomous agent improver, can directly edit the weights of a small language model, Qwen3.5-0.8B, to reduce looping behavior and increase accuracy on math problems from about 7% to over 37% without executing the model. This approach builds on prior work where GPT-6 Astra edited model weights to improve performance, and combining both edits raised accuracy to nearly 59%. Beaker identifies specific neurons responsible for problematic loops and adjusts their outputs to enhance model responses, achieving similar improvements at lower computational cost compared to previous methods. Beaker operates by proposing weight changes, scoring them against training examples, and retaining edits that yield measurable gains, iterating until no further improvements are found. It can function with or without direct model reads, relying on feedback from scored answers rather than running the model itself. The experiments show that weight-space programming can effectively modify model behavior, such as shortening answers or reducing repetitive tokens, though some behaviors like teaching the model to admit uncertainty remain challenging. This technique suggests a path toward continual learning where models autonomously refine themselves by editing their own parameters.

items.title: LiteLLM rewrites its Router component in Rust, replacing over 50,000 lines of Python code to improve performance and reliability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: LiteLLM has replaced its Router component's Python implementation with a Rust core as of version 1.110.0, consolidating routing logic including retries, fallbacks, and deployment selection into a single source. This rewrite aims to enable faster message processing by December and introduces a new router playground for exploring routing configurations. The migration involved first refactoring the Python code to maintain backward compatibility before swapping in the Rust core, ensuring no regressions despite the complexity of routing interactions with databases, Redis, and inference endpoints. The new router interface segments functionality into clear, mostly immutable subsets, improving efficiency and code clarity while deprecating the old interface by the end of the month. LiteLLM employed differential testing to verify that the Rust implementation matches the behavior of the previous Python router, preserving correctness and handling complex edge cases around retries and overrides. This careful approach reflects lessons from past software rewrites to avoid losing valuable, battle-tested logic.

items.title: Sequoia Capital invests hundreds of millions in AI holding company Sequence to fund acquisitions in insurance and other industries [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Sequoia Capital is investing hundreds of millions of dollars into Sequence Holding, a one-year-old company that recently announced a $7.7 billion insurance acquisition co-led by Michael Dell's family office. Sequence is part of a new category of holding companies that acquire businesses in established sectors like accounting and insurance and aim to integrate AI to replace or complement human work. The new funding from Sequoia is expected to enable Sequence to pursue additional acquisitions as it continues scouting targets.

items.title: TechCrunch: Many announced data center projects may never be built amid permitting delays, local opposition, and electricity shortages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: The data center industry is facing significant challenges including local opposition, permitting delays, and a shortage of electricity, which are hindering the construction of new facilities. Beyond these issues, many announced data center projects may never progress to construction, raising concerns about the viability of AI infrastructure investments. TechCrunch's Equity podcast features Brent Nelson from Ascend Analytics discussing how to distinguish between data center projects likely to be completed and those that remain speculative. This analysis is crucial as billions of dollars are invested in AI infrastructure, and understanding which projects will materialize affects planning and market expectations.

items.title: Data center projects face delays from local opposition, permitting issues, and power shortages; many announced AI infrastructure plans may never be built
items.content_text: The data center expansion driven by AI infrastructure investment is encountering significant obstacles including local resistance, permitting delays, and electricity supply challenges. Many proposed projects may not proceed to construction, raising concerns about the accuracy of the current data center pipeline. Experts highlight that only a fraction of announced data center projects are likely to be completed, with permitting reforms needed to address administrative bottlenecks. Energy reliability issues, such as the limitations of natural gas during extreme weather, further complicate development, prompting consideration of alternatives like battery storage paired with grid connections. These challenges suggest that without policy changes and improved infrastructure planning, the data center boom supporting AI growth could slow, impacting developers and the broader technology ecosystem.

items.title: CoreWeave shifts to customer prepayments and shorter contracts to finance AI infrastructure growth amid rising prices and debt concerns [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: CoreWeave is changing its financing strategy to support its AI infrastructure expansion by increasingly requiring upfront customer payments, borrowing against specific contracts, and pursuing shorter-term deals that allow for higher pricing. The company reported $3.66 billion in revenue for the third quarter, up 168% year-over-year, but also posted a $709 million net loss and $846 million in interest expenses, prompting a move away from unsecured debt toward loans backed by customer contracts. The company expects about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits in the next three months, including over $3 billion from new contracts for existing capacity. CoreWeave has raised prices by 25% in July and another 10% later in the quarter, with further increases planned, and is allocating more capacity to short-term contracts that command higher prices. While this approach could improve cash flow and profitability, it carries risks related to contract renewals and pricing stability amid uncertain future demand.

items.title: Meta's infrastructure chief Santosh Janardhan to leave early next year amid AI data center expansion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Meta Platforms announced that Santosh Janardhan, its longtime head of global infrastructure, will step down and leave the company early next year. The leadership change comes as Meta undertakes a massive buildout of data centers to support its AI initiatives. Janardhan's departure marks a significant transition in the management of Meta's extensive data center operations during a critical period of AI infrastructure growth.

items.title: Hugging Face releases 207 versioned WebGPU kernels for local AI inference with benchmarking tool Fleet [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Hugging Face has launched @huggingface/kernels, a library providing 207 optimized WebGPU kernels for running AI operations directly in browsers. Each kernel is published as a versioned package with interfaces, shader templates, correctness tests, and benchmarks to support efficient local AI processing across diverse hardware. The release includes Fleet, a browser-based GPU benchmarking suite that crowdsources performance and correctness data from users' devices to improve kernel variants and optimize execution on real-world GPUs. This effort aims to enhance browser inference speed and reliability by making GPU operations individually testable and adaptable to different devices and browsers.

items.title: Fractile raises $720 million Series C led by Britain's Sovereign AI Fund, valuing the AI chip startup over $7 billion [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Fractile, a British startup developing AI chips, has secured $720 million in a Series C funding round led by Britain's Sovereign AI Fund to strengthen the UK's position in AI hardware. The company aims to ship its first chips and systems next year, focusing on a unique hardware design that stacks DRAM on top of each chip to improve memory capacity and speed for large language models. Fractile's approach includes a full-stack solution with a machine learning compiler to optimize AI model execution on its chips. The funding round, which also involved Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Redpoint, values the company at over £5 billion (approximately $7 billion). This positions Fractile among the top-funded startups competing in the purpose-built AI chip market, addressing the growing demand for efficient AI inference hardware amid increasing model complexity.

AI Inference Startups Are Quietly Buying Their Own Chips [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: The fast-growing crop of startups that lease computing capacity from cloud firms and then resell it, without spending a nickel on their own AI chips, are at a crossroads. Finding it harder to line up enough computing capacity to serve their customers, some are starting to buy their own chips, which is likely to drastically change the economics of their business. The difficulty in getting enough compute also has pushed some of these startups to look for computational resources from dozens of smaller neoclouds, which tend to have more available capacity than larger hyperscalers such as Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud Platform. News this week of a hack of Fireworks, one of the best known of these startups, highlights the risk of that approach.

items.title: Introducing The Information's 50 Most Promising Startups of 2026
items.content_text: As artificial intelligence changes how companies get hacked, investors are paying up for startups that promise to keep defenders ahead. That dynamic shaped this year's The Information 50, our annual list of the most promising startups. For the first time, our list includes a category devoted solely to security, and it holds some of the list's biggest bets. Two of the four most highly valued companies in this seventh edition of the list are security startups valued at more than $1 billion apiece, and six of the security firms are run by Israelis, which have a long history of breakout hits in this field. At a time when many people use AI to research new companies, our reporters didn't use AI to find candidates. They just had good ol' fashioned conversations with dozens of founders and investors-including many that pointed us to startups they missed out on-and collected hard data on revenue and growth rates at the companies. You can view the list here, and join our conference call for The Information subscribers at 12pm PT / 3pm ET to discuss the list with several of the founders whose companies are on it.

items.title: llm 0.37.2 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Release: llm 0.37.2 Fixes a security issue reported by Daniel de Araujo in GHSA-v9h7-jj4g-f862 and GHSA-r639-rr7r-x72w. LLM has a mechanism called extra-openai-models.yaml - now managed by the new-in-0.37 llm openai endpoint add command - for using LLM with OpenAI-compatible API endpoints from other providers. Daniel reported two ways this could accidentally send your configured OpenAI API key to one of those providers: if the key named by api_key_name had never been stored, or if a responses: true model was run with -o chat_completions 1. items.title: Anthropic's PE-Backed Venture, Ode, Pushes to Get Paid for AI Results [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Private equity firms and AI labs are sorting out how to charge clients and hire enough engineers for joint ventures they've launched to build custom AI tools for businesses. That comes as private equity firms are looking to the technology to boost profits, including at companies they've struggled to sell. One such team-up is Ode with Anthropic, which launched in July with $1.5 billion in capital commitments from investors including Blackstone and Hellman & Friedman. Ode currently charges most of the several dozen businesses it works with a fixed fee to develop and launch custom AI products, people familiar with the partnership say. The company lets clients retain ownership of the AI software it builds, the people said, allowing them to keep using or even sell the tools once completed without paying Ode ongoing fees. Those terms help Ode attract customers that balked at the terms offered by the team of engineers at Anthropic that embeds with enterprises, which seeks to retain ownership of the custom software it builds and license it back to customers, one of the people said. But Ode has been looking at other ways to earn more on AI projects. Some Ode executives initially proposed coinvesting in companies that were also its customers, but Blackstone's team pushed back on the idea, one of the people said. Instead, Ode decided to charge performance-based bonus fees on top of the fixed project fees, allowing it to earn more if clients hit specific financial targets. Less than 10% of Ode's clients are paying those performance-based fees, one of the people said, though Ode is aiming to grow that share. Setting the fees can be difficult because the company and its customers both need to agree on how to measure any AI-driven gains, including setting a baseline and financial or product-related goals. The fees may be negotiated once a contract is signed and Ode then does some early exploratory work and collects data, giving both sides enough information to set terms before moving on to the building phase, the people said. Ode inherited some of its business from Fractional AI, a startup founded in 2024 that the venture acquired in May for an undisclosed sum. Fractional already worked mostly with private equity-backed companies to automate tasks and build custom AI software, and Fractional co-founders Chris Taylor and Eddie Siegel became Ode's CEO and chief technology officer, respectively. One of those clients, risk and compliance software company LogicGate, paid a fixed fee in the low seven figures for a project that began under Fractional last summer and finished this fall, said LogicGate CEO Diego Panama. (LogicGate's backers include growth equity firm PSG, which led the company's $113 million funding round in 2021.) Ode engineers built a custom agent that shortened LogicGate's client onboarding from 120 days to 90 days or less. LogicGate received full intellectual property ownership and training to run the tool independently, Panama said, and it subsequently began selling the agent to other businesses and has signed several deals. The agent is set to launch publicly at the end of the month. Around half of Ode's clients are software or business services companies, while the rest come from industrial and other sectors. Its client base is split roughly equally between portfolio companies of Ode's backers, including at least six Blackstone companies, and other businesses. All of the Blackstone portfolio companies working with Ode currently pay fixed fees, including accounting firm Citrin Cooperman, where Ode engineers built a new onboarding system, similar to the work they did at LogicGate. Blackstone typically sets targets to improve earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization in a specific division when evaluating how an AI project is working. Other AI services firms are experimenting with similar fee structures. Hyde, backed by Bain Capital Ventures and General Catalyst, launched last year and helps businesses build custom AI models using their own data. Clients then own the customer models and can run them themselves or pay Hyde to host them. Hyde typically assigns two engineers to work with clients for around four weeks per project, charging for that work plus a recurring fee for using its software platform. (Clients also pay for compute based on usage.) Around half its contracted revenue includes a portion of fees tied to results-its fee for an automotive client, for example, is tied to whether agents meet certain car sales goals. Hyde CEO Anirudh Sanga said demand for Hyde's services has roughly doubled monthly for the past three months. At the same time, a shortage of engineers is limiting how much business AI services firms can take on. Anthropic itself has sought to address the shortage, announcing a $100 million effort last month to train 10,000 deployment engineers at customer and partner companies by the end of next year. Upstart AI services firms are also competing with major tech firms for talent. Microsoft in July committed $2.5 billion to its Microsoft Frontier Co. with the aim of placing 6,000 engineers inside enterprise customers, partnering with consultancies like Accenture and EY. As of November 2025, Fractional had an annual revenue run rate of over $12 million. At the time of the May acquisition, it was generating around $30 million in ARR, which has since nearly tripled, according to people familiar with the matter. But Ode is being selective about the clients it takes on because it doesn't have enough engineers to handle all potential business, one of the people said, though it has enough demand for at least two to three times its current workload. OpenAI Deployment Co. has faced similar constraints. The venture, backed by TPG and other investment firms including Brookfield Asset Management and Bain Capital, has sought to hire more engineers to expand available capacity. Ode has made several acquihires and acquisitions since launching, including one of Casper Studios, which designed specialized AI products using Claude. Ode remains open to exploring more deals, a person familiar with the venture said, but is looking to expand its services or geographic reach instead of simply adding more people. Hyde, for its part, isn't currently seeking acquisitions, but it has declined several takeover offers, Sanga said, mostly from large companies looking to quickly establish their own AI deployment team. Fintech and Crypto Startups to Watch Each year, The Information picks 50 startups that have the potential to be breakout stars. This time around, our fintech and crypto category featured new twists on trading and betting and startups positioned to benefit from growth in emerging areas like agentic payments. There's Fomo, a viral trading app that plans to branch out from memecoins to tokenized stocks, and Catalyst, a startup offering agents that help people trade across venues like prediction markets and crypto exchanges. On the payments side, Natural is offering bank accounts for AI agents, while stablecoin-backed card provider Kast is expanding beyond retail customers by courting merchants. items.title: Anthropic, Others Warn of AI Acceleration [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: In recent weeks, my colleagues and I have been trying our hand at being venture capitalists: today, the end result of that process is our annual list of the 50 most promising startups of this year, published today. We've had a pretty good track record in past years: AI startups we've previously highlighted include OpenRouter, when the model-routing startup was valued at $500 million; Cursor, when the coding agent was valued at $400 million; and Perplexity, when the AI-powered search engine was valued at $150 million. OpenRouter was recently acquired by Stripe for more than $7 billion, Cursor in August was acquired by SpaceX for $60 billion, and Perplexity was most recently raising at a more than $30 billion valuation. Each year, however, it gets more difficult to pick promising AI startups that fall within our requirements of having raised less than $100 million and being valued less than $1 billion. These days, it feels like the moment any young AI company has a hint of revenue traction, investors are all over them. Still, we've managed to uncover a number of under-the-radar gems in this year's list. In fact, we had trouble whittling down the entrants for our AI infrastructure and security categories, which included everything from companies that help developers train their models using multiple cloud providers to those that use AI to protect employees' devices. Such companies have become even more important as the rate of AI-powered cyberattacks have increased.-Stephanie Palazzolo Now, onto today's column... AI researchers that focus on ensuring AI doesn't harm humans have reason to be a little rattled. Two recent reports suggest AI is advancing even more quickly than previously thought, and that's increased these safety researchers' worries that AI will escape human control to wreak havoc.

items.title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention. Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself, allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues, where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments. items.title: How should authors handle a suspected auto-generated review at ICLR? Flag to the AC or just rebut? [D] [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: An author at ICLR is concerned about a review they suspect to be auto-generated by AI. The review gave a low score with low confidence, while other reviewers gave higher scores with high confidence. An AI detection tool flagged the review as likely AI-generated, and the author noticed the review's weaknesses focus on appendix material. The author plans to address all points in the rebuttal and seeks advice on whether to confidentially inform the Area Chair (AC), what evidence ACs consider credible regarding AI-generated reviews, the influence of low-confidence reviews on meta-reviews, and experiences with flagging AI-generated reviews.
